prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms confined at the magic wavelength enable measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler, recoil and, to first order, light-shift errors for thousands of atoms at once. That is a clean idea that is also a clean experiment. It was demonstrated first with strontium and then driven by Ye's group, with its record stability and systematic control, into the 1e-18 regime. The result is not an instrument for its own sake. At this precision one resolves the gravitational redshift over millimetres, searches for variation of constants and ultralight dark matter, and prepares a redefinition of the second. I judge the atomic physics behind the claims with some confidence, because the systematics (blackbody shift, higher-order lattice shifts, collisions) are well understood and the clock comparisons across JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST agree. The attribution is the cleanest on our list: one concept and first demonstration, one decisive realisation of the accuracy. The two credited names carry both. Of the shortlist it is the candidate I can check most directly, and the field is not controversial.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one I raised myself. A lattice clock is a measurement technique that follows the frequency comb prize (2005) and the ion-trap prize (2012), and one can ask whether this is an incremental step on the same road rather than something nature surprised us with. Ye's cavity-stabilised-laser and comb work also overlaps with the 2005 recognition, and Lemonde, Takamoto and the NIST and PTB groups have a real claim to be named. Beyond that, the most dramatic science that lattice clocks promise (a new definition of the second, constraints on dark matter) is still mostly ahead of us. I also have a stake in my own field: as an atomic theorist I may overvalue precision, and I should not confuse that taste with the committee's mandate.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B042 first, treats it as a measurement-technique breakthrough that has opened relativistic geodesy, constants tests and the redefinition of the second, and flags that the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes could make it look incremental.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking and on the attribution, and I do not think the incremental worry is decisive. The comb gave us a way to count optical cycles. The lattice clock gave us a new regime of accuracy and stability, because the magic wavelength lets many atoms be interrogated at once without the ion clock's single-particle statistics. That changed what can be measured, for example redshift across millimetres. I would add a qualification to the question you left open: Ye's role should be described as the realisation at record accuracy together with the many-body and cavity-aided extensions, not as comb work, so that the citation does not re-credit 2005. Lemonde and Takamoto are the names I would most like us to discuss in the footnote.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B032) first as a decades-long instrument-driven discovery of a new window, and B042 second as a mature, timely precision tool, while asking whether Ye's role is the decisive realisation or one of several leading groups.
responses.response: I take the IceCube case seriously and I defer to you and Ulf on astroparticle matters. My hesitation is that the discovery claim is strong for the diffuse flux but individual sources are still at 3-4 sigma, and the 2002 prize already covered cosmic neutrinos. On your question about Ye: I think the decisive step was not merely leading a good group. He took the Katori concept to the stability and accuracy that made the 1e-18 comparison possible, and his group's measurements are the ones the others are compared against. If the committee does not accept that, a Katori-only prize is a real alternative to discuss, but I would not choose it because it understates a joint realisation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B019) first as a clean example of theory anticipating a new quantum state, with experiment following and reproduced by many groups.
responses.response: I share your taste for results that overturn expectations, and B019 is the strongest condensed-matter candidate in my view. My reservations are about maturity and attribution rather than quality. The pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, which is why I would not call it settled. The experimental credit also runs to Yuan Cao and others, which three credited names cannot reflect. I cannot judge the finer theory arguments as well as you can, so I keep it as an alternative and not as my first choice, and would revisit it if you can show that the phases themselves are now well understood.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B049) first as a new light-matter regime that became the common language of superconducting devices, and notes that four credited names exceed the three-person limit and that the 2025 prize is a natural predecessor.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged your own closeness to this community. Circuit QED is mature and widely reproduced, and I see the logic of it as a follow-up to the 2025 prize. Two things hold me back. First, the credited-name problem is serious: Blais's theory is as decisive as Girvin's, and a clean three-person split cuts a real contributor. Second, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits has just been awarded, so a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon seems to me worth avoiding unless the committee thinks the discovery content is distinctly different. I would put B049 in the next tier, not in my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee counts optical clocks as a discovery about nature or as a metrology instrument, and so whether the Nobel will's wording is met comfortably.
Whether Takamoto, Lemonde or the early NIST and PTB lattice-clock contributors are material enough to unsettle a Katori and Ye pair.
How much the 2005 and 2012 prizes should count against a third precision-spectroscopy prize in two decades.
My own recollection of the earliest independent lattice-clock demonstrations is not precise and should be checked against the record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for Katori and Ye: I am not aware of a collaboration, shared institution or supervisory link with either. I note for transparency that I am a theoretical atomic physicist working in an adjacent AMO area and am a long-time collaborator of the 2023 laureate Anne L'Huillier, though that is not a connection to any shortlisted candidate. I also collaborate with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, which are not on this shortlist.
